utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Sachdeva will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence until it's complete. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I'm going to be very --

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- Today. Paragraph 32 of your statement you speak about the order which is Exhibit P2014 and that is the order of the Pristina command dated the 25th of May, 1999, and I'd like to ask the registrar to bring that up on to the screen; and I'm going to ask you a few questions about that document. If we could go to -- firstly, you recognise this order, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English. Now, at the top of page 2 you'll see it reads: "Engage armed non-Siptar civilians to secure vital facilities and communications to protect and defend the local population." And my question is: These armed non-Siptar civilians were for the most part locally armed Serbs by the Serb forces that were assisting in combat operations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to point out this. We see the date in the header of this order. This order was never implemented, although it was in fact delivered to the units. Secondly, I would like to point out this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- unarmed non-Siptar population, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Madic, yes that's what we want you to tell us about, what does that mean? It's a simple question. You don't need to tell us anything else. Just tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer this question simply because these armed units are not something that I had as part of in my units nor was I aware of the existence of any such armed units in my surroundings. As I had none, there was no way that I could dispatch them to wherever my own unit was performing combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, General, at the end of this order - and you'll remember that paragraph 14 at the end of the order places you as the commander of the 252nd Armoured Brigade in charge of the planning, organizing, and conducting of combat operations. So when you received this order, leaving aside that you say it was not implemented, when you saw that term "engage armed non-Siptars," what did it mean to you as someone who was responsible -- who would have been responsible for the planning of these operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the order was never implemented. Secondly, in that order there's a particular item about tasks for units. A task in this order was defined also for my brigade, and it doesn't say anywhere unarmed -- it doesn't say anywhere armed non-Siptar population; therefore I believe myself to be under no obligation in relation to any such armed units. They never reported to me nor was in fact I aware that there were any such units existing near me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'm sorry I have to persist. As I've already mentioned, you were placed in charge of the implementation of this order, and in fact it is a direct -- I suggest to you it is a direct order to engage the armed non-Siptar civilians. So do you agree at least that it means that those, for the most part, those locally -- the local Serbs in those villages were to be engaged by the military in combat operations? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I believe we've covered this ground at least twice before, and now my learned friend is asking the same question over again. Likewise, there is the implication, the following implication, in my learned friend's question: "I suggest to you it is a direct order, "and so on and so forth, whereas the general has already explained what exactly the order contains in item 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree strongly with that proposition. The witness has not answered the question and the question can be pursued. Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, do you remember the question or should I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The question is this: This instruction to engage armed non-Siptar civilians is an instruction to engage for the most part those local Serbs from those villages by the military, by the VJ, by the MUP and for them to be used in combat operations. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is your right to make suggestions such as these, but I simply can't confirm that. Nothing like that ever happened throughout my three months in Kosovo and Metohija. As to item 14 of the order, as you have explained, it says that the 252nd Mechanised Brigade -- Armoured Brigade must organize coordinated action, but this was never implemented. It was withdrawn for that precise reason. The brigade was in no position to organize all these things in the broader area, and especially not in an area that was outside of its area of responsibility. We were unable to establish any sort of contact with our neighbours, let alone exercise command over any particular combat operations. Therefore, once again, this order was in fact never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Again, let's leave aside that fact. Presumably when General Lazarevic wrote this order he had the impression that it could have been implemented. Now, when you received this order, weren't you at least curious as to what this phrase "engage the armed non-Siptars" meant as a commander, as someone who was responsible for the implementation of this order?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when you receive an order from one of your superior officers in the VJ there's a procedure called understanding your tasks. One thing you do is you look for where your unit belongs and where you belong in that particular task. Once you've understood the position of your unit, all you care about are the adjacent units and nothing else. Given the fact that armed non-Siptar population is not something that I had in my units or anywhere near me, it just wasn't something that I was looking at at the time. I had enough on my plate as I was, and I certainly was in no position, or for that matter, able to deal with this, it simply would have been too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, is it correct to say that you were put in charge of planning the coordination among units for the execution of this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we look at item 14 of this order, we shall see that there is a contradiction there. One cannot have a brigade implementing combat operations, especially if that task was not specified in the previous item of the corps commander's order, and that was why the order was never carried out. I had no equipment and no ability at all to organize a combat operation of this sort, and that was the reason the order was never implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now answer my question. Is it correct to say that you were supposed to be in charge of planning the coordination among units for the execution of this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to item 14 of the order, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you got this order, did you scratch your head and wonder: How the hell am I going to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did it never cross your mind to think: Who are hell are the armed non-Siptar civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were any in areas covered by other units, then those units were the ones that were to involve them as their neighbours or as units within their own respective combat dispositions. I simply spent no time wondering about that because this didn't relate to me. I never had a unit like that, and this was not one of my problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the planning of this action, would it not have been important to know how many of them there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply didn't go into that. I received the order with some delay because the liaison officer who had gone on to get it--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Would it not be important to know how many of them there were? If you were actually going to carry this out - we know you didn't - but if you were, would it not have been important to know how many of them there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was no way I could know how many establishment units there were that were supposed to carry out this task, in the sense of manpower and equipment that could be used for fighting, let alone this other unit that you have been referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Move to something else, please, Mr. Sachdeva. That seems to be all we're going to get on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, my last topic. If we go to item 5 of this order, and that's page 5 of the English and page -- page 3 of the B/C/S, and actually it's a similar question to the ones I've been asking you, but again this order tasks you as the commander of the 252nd Armoured Brigade to engage in combat activity with the PJP, special police unit, and the JSO, special operations unit. And the question is: What did you do in terms of establishing that coordination and cooperation with the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what I don't see defined here is which unit this is about. This is a very generic term; that is what I was unclear about. This is a very generic term as used in relation to police, as if, for example, it said just VJ, whereas of course the VJ actually comprises a lot of smaller units. But the order arrived late, or rather, I received it late and I was unable to establish contact with these units. Therefore, I didn't even know which units would be operating on this task alongside the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little bit confused by that answer. You said you didn't know which units they referred to, but then you also say you were unable to establish contact with the units. So did you actually attempt to establish contact with these units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not according to the order. A very generic word is used there. According to what it says, I was to establish contact with whoever was in command of the police forces at the upper-most level. As for the armed forces, I was unable to establish contact with the upper-most levels. Somebody ought to have told me which unit this was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, General, in your statement you say, as you've told the Court, that this order was not implemented; however, the action took place, and there was co-activity and good cooperation existing between the two structures. So when the action took place, how did you ensure that this cooperation continued between the VJ and the police? Who did you speak to? What did you speak about? How was that cooperation done?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was not carried out. There was another order that was carried out which arrived later bearing different date for readiness. The cooperation with the police occurred in the following way: I called an officer from the corps command who was in charge of planning this operation, as defined in the other order; and I asked this officer to get in touch with the police with their own officer in order to have coordination, concerted action, and cooperation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who was the person in the police that was contacted?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was the particular police unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant commander of the 122nd Detachment of the PJP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And as the commander of this operation, did you yourself meet with members of this detachment and explain what was to take place?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met and on that occasion he said that he had his own mission which had been assigned to him by his superiors. He also said that he would carry it out independently and that he would be one of my brigade's neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in that meeting you had, how did you -- what was it that you discussed with respect to the joint or the -- sorry, the cooperation and the coordinated activity?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went on to define his own axis of operations. He said who would be the right-hand neighbour of my unit, and I told him about my own axis. I told him about his left-hand neighbour. We set the time at which we would achieve readiness for the start of combat activity. The time had already been set by the corps command order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that as a member of the military and given that combat is the specialty of the military, if there was a disagreement or if there was a conflict between planning, your, the military's, decision and method in conducting that combat would take precedence over the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the police had their own mission, they had their own axis of operations, and they had their own ultimate objective. And by the time they got there, their activities had already been planned, objected. My situation was difficult because my unit equipment didn't actually have the equipment and weapons that it would have been supposed to have, but rather I had to use combat vehicle crews, take some of their members, and our planning was separate. The only thing that had been set for us was the deadline at which this activity was to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, presumably the objective was the same for the military and the police in terms of the overall operation. So if there was a disagreement between the military and the police, is my understanding correct that the military -- that the method suggested by the military would prevail; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my activity had been planned by the time I got there. The police officer's activity had been planned by the time he got there. My mission was separate from the mission that the police had as their ultimate objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, if there had been separate plans and your tasks had been defined in the police's tasks had been defined, what was the point in the cooperation then? Why did you need to meet?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to meet, above all, in order to define the time for readiness to begin this activity, to define the axes along which the units would have been brought there in order to keep ourselves from getting our wires crossed and in order to have some coordination and concerted action because we were actual neighbours, weren't we.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at this meeting, how many members of the military were there, and how many members of the police were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven or eight military, three or four police officers, not counting the security people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you were discussing the forthcoming operation, did you refer in the briefing, did you refer to a common map or a common order?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a decision map containing the decision of the Pristina Corps command. I showed them how the operation had been envisaged. However, they refused to play along with that map and said -- and the way the operation was portrayed on the map, they said had they had their own axis of operations and that they could not act within the same framework as the army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say they said they had their own axis of operations and their own plan, this is something they told you or did they show you a specific plan and order?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said they had their own axis and their own ultimate objective ones, once that objective was achieved they would move on to their next mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your -- tell me if my understanding is correct, in this briefing you're referring to a common -- you're referring to an order and a map discussing an upcoming operation and some of them -- the police tells you they had their own plans. What was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reaction was to accept what they said. We were of the same rank. I had to come to terms with their mission. Other than that, it suited me just fine that they should have their own axis of operations so we did not have to operate together but rather separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, you were about to go into combat with the police in a coordinated action and you are giving a briefing and the police tell you they had their own plans. Did you not even ask to see those plans? Didn't you feel it was important to you as someone who was planning the operation, to find out what those plans were?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of that unit had sufficient authority to tell me, to inform me about his own axis of operations and to tell me about their ultimate objective, what the line was that they were supposed to reach and what mission they he had been assigned. I wasn't authorised to ask him to hand over their documents to me so that I might then check whether they were all right or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's not a question of handing over documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sachdeva, how much more are you going to pursue this? You are --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Not much further, not much further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- well over the time that was suggested. Is there any other topic that needs to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, when this action was actually carried out, and indeed prior to the order being issued to you which you could not implement, do you understand that there had been coordination of planning between VJ and MUP representatives at a higher level than you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I was able to assume based on the documents that I received. Whenever there was joint activity, the task was to lend support to forces of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The order which you were asked about, P2014, you say contains language which you don't really understand, that's the armed non-Siptar civilians. It contains a direction at the end which you say could not be implemented because of the general state of readiness of the combat units involved. The order seems a bit of a mess. Is that your impression of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This order was signed by Mr. Lazarevic -- General Lazarevic. We've had quite a number of witnesses in this court tell us what a professional officer he was. Can you account for him making such a hash of an order?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe he was the one who made a hash of it. Probably he was not aware of the situation that prevailed in my unit, and he wasn't aware of the fact that I wasn't able to establish contact with all those units that were supposed to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to try and be clear about the circumstances when you came into Kosovo. If you have your report -- your statement in front of you, we can perhaps focus on paragraphs 7 and 8. You refer in paragraph 7 to part of the brigade being relocated to Kosovo on the 20th of March, but you've also given us in the course of your evidence the date the 16th of March. What was it that happened on the 16th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its composition under the order on measures of constant combat-readiness, the brigade had a group which corresponded to a weakened battalion. In mid-March, as I said yesterday, this unit was resubordinated to the command of the 125th Motorised Brigade. I believe the order stipulated that it was about checking mobilisational and combat-readiness of that unit, that is, combat group, which is a standing unit in army units under the order on measures of constant combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that was removed from your command and resubordinated at that stage to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the 125th Brigade, and the brigade was subordinated to the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You then say that on the 20th of March what ultimately became the 252nd Tactical Group was redeployed to Kosovo. Now, on the 20th of March, was it already designated as the 252nd Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two armoured battalions that were transferred by the 20th of March were units that were temporarily subordinated to the command of the 252nd Armoured Brigade in February. They were not called the 252nd Tactical Group at the time when you are asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, when were they designated the 252nd Tactical Group? I think when combined with a command support units and combat activity security units.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalions were independent with their commands, and as such they could be subordinated to any unit as long as they had a superior command above them. When the command was formed with the tactical units that I stated in my statement, then they got the name 252nd Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can reckon from the 23rd March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At that stage, were you their commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of the order of the army, I was temporarily sent to be the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Simultaneously, did you remain commander of the 252nd Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not simultaneously discharge both functions, but I was appointed to be the commander of that 252nd Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your statement you tell us that by the 17th of February you were commander of the 252nd Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you stop being commander of that when you're commander of the tactical group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a person is temporarily sent to work in a different unit, then his competencies in the originating unit cease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there's a period during which you command the 252nd Tactical Group but do not command the 252nd Armoured Brigade; have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 23rd March until 5th April, I was commander of the 252nd Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why was the change made on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The change occurred because Colonel Jovanovic Miodrag was temporarily sent to the command of the Pristina Corps, who was able to take over as commander of the tactical group, and he was qualified enough; and since the 252nd Armoured Brigade was deprived of its commander by establishment, I returned to my duties as commander by establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 252nd Armoured Brigade was, according to your statement, resubordinated to the Pristina Corps on the 29th of March. When resubordination of that nature takes place, do orders require to be made both by the corps from which the brigade is moving and by the corps to which it is moving?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just to complete the position in relation to the 252nd Tactical Group, are you aware of very serious allegations of criminal acts by members of the 252nd Tactical Group in the course of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the location Mali Alas in Lipljan municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it is a place name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're not aware of allegations of the murder of 20 Albanians there by a group from the 252nd Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could look now, please, at paragraph 42 of your statement which I think is a reference to a military territorial detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that detachment was resubordinated to your brigade. Can you give us examples -- specific examples of the tasks they undertook while resubordinated to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary task of this detachment was to secure roads, passes, and crossings that were susceptible -- that were liable to be used by terrorist forces to cross over from one area to another because the unit was composed of local people who knew all the tracks and shortcuts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. What do you mean by "secure" these various facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean primarily that they were supposed to make sure that roads are passable. It often happened to us that roads, being long, could be mined. So we set up forces to guard such stretches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do they stand on the road and guard it? Do they drive along the road? Or what do they do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their positions overlooking roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they could be concealed overlooking the roads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And beyond securing routes, did they do anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes they could be engaged in combat activities because they had particular kinds of weapons, such as mortars 59-millimetres, and we had no such weapons. We could not move large weapons systems. And the brigade did not have enough personnel to conduct combat activities because the personnel of my brigade had the kind of equipment that requires the constant presence of crews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recollect the strength of the 101st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that the only detachment subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, re -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I do have one question arising from your questions, and the reason why is the issue of Mali Alas. I was going to raise it yesterday; however, the answers of the witness made -- made me make a decision otherwise. However, now that it's raised, I would like to put one document to the witness with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry, I want to show you one document, and that is 3D1061. And this is a document from the 3rd Army security department and it pertains to the incident in Mali Alas in April 1999. And if you look at the bottom in the handwritten notes, you will see that it states, if the English can be scrolled down, please. You'll see in the second sentence, and I'll read it: "The facts point to the conclusion that the crime may have been committed by members of the TG, tactical group, of the 252nd Armoured Brigade ..." So the question is that your brigade is mentioned in this document and I want to ask you that upon seeing this is it still your evidence that you know nothing about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, with your leave I would kindly ask my learned friend to read the entire passage without skipping certain words because the result is something taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the point that's being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the sentence -- the full sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, do read the full sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: "The facts point to the conclusion that the crime may have been committed by members of the 252nd Tactical Group of the 252nd Armoured Brigade, but also by units of /illegible/ from Lipljan," and then it goes on to say: "There is no information as to whether they were requested to give documents, statements (Ilic) et cetera." Your unit is not mentioned in the 3rd Army security department report, and again I ask you: Do you maintain your evidence that you had no idea about these allegations during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I would like to respond to what is written here. Whoever wrote the tactical group from the 252nd Armoured Brigade did not know the situation, and I believe that person to have been militarily ignorant because it's not a tactical group of the 252nd Armoured Brigade, it's an independent tactical group with its own chain of command. It was in a -- on a separate route at quite a distance from us. I had no private, let alone, official contacts that would enable me to know what was going on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, it's just a very simple question, and this person is from the 3rd Army, so he's not someone who's unfamiliar with military matters. This document does not change your testimony? You had no idea of these allegations, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, let him answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no knowledge about that, and I keep saying that the tactical group was an independent unit, it was not part of the 252nd Armoured Brigade. I stated that yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I see the next page of this document, please? Both -- can we have the B/C/S also. So the initials are at the bottom. I'm sorry. So who has actually signed that document, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "Chief, Colonel Stojadin Antic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's who it's addressed to. Who has actually written it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the Serbian text only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does it look as though it was written by Branko Gajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I can see, it is addressed to Branko Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the actual report appears to be made by Colonel Antic to Gajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then there seems to be a draft letter in reply at the bottom, a proposed reply; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot read the text well, but there are things noted here in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know who General Gajic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe he was one of the senior officers in the security administration, but from this very text we can see he worked in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic -- sorry -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Mr. President. Just with respect to the last name on this document I have to ask the witness one question with your leave. I note that it seems to have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, you'll see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, tell me what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The question is that at the end of the document it appears that the letter has been sent to the -- someone in his security department in the 252nd Armoured Brigade, and I wanted to ask him whether he knows this person and whether the witness maintains the evidence that he had not heard about those allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, so this letter shows what? A letter sent to who in the 252nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we move to the last page of the English, please, it says that: "The letter to the 1st army OB" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we can read that for ourselves. Your cross-examination is complete. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If you allow me, just for the record I want to clarify certain points. My learned friend from the Prosecution referred to a document and what was written in a document, but I believe it is necessary to state that the handwritten passage on that document was put to the witness, not the document itself. And now I would like to ask a couple of questions, and just for the sake of clarity next week witnesses will be coming who will provide much more information about Mali Alas and who will make the picture much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it's me again. Good morning. Have you ever seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up another document, 3D1059.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was it you saw it before?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he answered no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer is recorded as yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you seen that document before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be useful for once. The previous document had been shown to that Gajic who had been heard as a witness, and that's when it was discussed before, just to remind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I call Exhibit Number 3D1059, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, my learned friend from the Prosecution put this document to you yesterday. My first question is: When did you see it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday [Realtime transcript read in error "yes"].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Look at the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25th June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is that after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who issued this document and to whom was it delivered?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was issued by the security department of the 3rd Army command, and it was addressed to the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff. One copy was left with the author and one with the security organ of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, you've just told us to whom it was delivered. Was anything delivered to your brigade, your corps, or your army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, if I might, at page 23, line 20 -- sorry, line 19, in answer to the question put I thought I heard a different answer from the witness than what's recorded. Could you clarify that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, for the record, when was the first time you saw the document that you see on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, the 23rd of January, 2008, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can the security organ institute criminal proceedings without your knowledge and without informing you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the organ -- the security organ is not duty-bound to report to me when instituting criminal proceedings. He can notify only his superior, and on this document on the stamp you can see 3rd Army command and then separately it says "security organ." And such seals are available only to the security organs not to the command organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do security organs have a separate chain of reporting?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In item 2 here we see, based on initial operative information. General, I know you're not a lawyer, nor have you ever worked in the security organs, but let me ask you, the document you see before you is it in fact a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only interpret it by its title which says: "Amendment to the report."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It says in the document that volunteers and reservists. Did you have any reservists, volunteers, on the 25th of June when this document was drawn up?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military conscripts labelled volunteers, I had those until the 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the 12th of June, did you have any authority over them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were released on the 12th of June, and after that I had no further authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, in one of your paragraphs, the one before the last, or rather, 48, you said that measures were taken to prevent the perpetration of crimes and to detect perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the security organ in your brigade or the security organs in your brigade, did they work intensively on this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs - and I told you yesterday in what units they were - did their job very intensively within the framework of their competencies. And I am very happy to have all perpetrators of crimes detected and prosecuted, especially serious crimes. And any document tending in that direction will contribute to clarifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, yesterday we mentioned the Supreme Defence Council; does it have a president at its head?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In war time was the president the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Constitution of the FRY in both peace and war, it's the president of the republic who is in command of the army in accordance with the decisions of the supreme council, and from this it follows that the president of the republic is at the same time the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's at the top. In view of your military experience and your rank, is it possible that there exists a collective organ of command within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, such a thing cannot exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to touch upon some issues raised by my learned friend. At one point you -- he mentioned that you were in command of the Drenica action, and you spoke about it in your statement. My question is: Were you in command of the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have been the commander of the action, and in item 14 of the order shown to me today it says I was only supposed to be in charge of planning, coordination, coordinated action, and cooperation. I was not in command of the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's clarify another point concerning Tactical Group 252 which was mentioned quite often. Can you tell me from what units -- out of what units that tactical group was composed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's already in the statement. Are you challenging that, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no need -- unless you're challenging paragraph 7, there's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But just -- with your leave just to clarify something I think that is not mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, ask the question to clarify. You don't need to go through the list before you do that. There's an awful amount of time wasted here repeating things that we already know, which you might have to set up if you had a jury determining your case; but where it's this group of Judges who have read the documents you don't need to go back over them to establish whether the witness knows something or not when he's said it in his statement. So if there's a particular point, focus on the particular point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am exerting the greatest efforts to make my examinations as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at paragraph 7 of your statement. It says here that there were two armoured battalions from the command of the 252nd were organized in Tactical Group 252. Were there also other units from other units of the army within the tactical group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After -- I'm speaking about up to the 5th of April, there was an armoured battalion from the 211th Armoured Brigade and one infantry battalion from the 2nd Infantry Brigade of the Nis Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could there be a pause between question and answer, please, the interpreter did not catch the beginning of the response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need that answer again, Mr. Cepic, because you overlapped -- or at least the witness spoke to quickly, I think. So can you deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to interpreters because I speeded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what other units were part of TG 252?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the period from the 23rd of March up to the 5th of April, 1999. Apart from the units listed in paragraph 7, the 252nd Tactical Group also included one armoured battalion from the 211th Armoured Brigade and an infantry battalion from the 2nd Infantry Brigade of the Nis Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you choose to confine it to the 5th of April because that's when you were no longer the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only provide information about that period. Later on, I don't know whether units were added on or taken away, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just to clarify a point. Yesterday you were asked a few questions about the agreement between the FRY and the OSCE and the verification mission. Do you perhaps recall and do you know whether this agreement referred to the entire territory of the country or only part of the territory, and did it affect your unit specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I held the post of brigade commander. This agreement was part of the defence policy which, according to the constitution, is conducted by the government. My knowledge was only of the nature of information and it did not directly affect my unit; so for that reason I was not interested in the details of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, you said that in wartime you met General Lazarevic, the commander of the Pristina Corps, two or three times. Do you perhaps remember that on one occasion you asked to be received by him and why?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. In April I was unable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I don't see, Mr. President, how this arises from my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It probably arises from questions I asked, though. Please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April, I was unable to comply with an order issued by the corps commander to report to him daily on the combat-readiness in my unit. Communication was through the sending of daily operative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Now, is there another matter that you wish to raise, Mr. Cepic, because this issue did not emerge from cross-examination or any other questions. If that's what you were after, then it was not an appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, just a brief question following from the previous.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did the system of communications -- was it difficult in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. There were even rumours that the commander had surrendered or was about to surrender, that there was a capitulation and I was cut off from everybody. I had no contacts, and I wanted to meet him at any cost to find out whether this was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was my last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Colonel Ljubomir Savic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, if I may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the next witness is brought in, I had a question about the statement I just wanted to inquire with the Court. There are a number of documents referred to in this statement that have not been translated; so I take it we will be proceeding in the same way as yesterday and that these documents will not be admitted into evidence until translations become available; is that correct?.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and indeed if you wish to take issue with whether any should be considered at all, then that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to call Mr. Usher just to pass this statement to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good morning. It's a pleasure to see you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you make a statement to the Defence team of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the document which is now before you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. That's the statement. The signatures are authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell me, please, if I were to put the same questions to you today that were put to you when you were making this statement, would you give the same answers to them today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this statement, it's 5D1392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, are you still in active duty service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm on active duty service, and I'm active in Nis in the command of the land forces of Serbia and my rank is colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at paragraph 4 of your statement, page 1.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Here you describe the action in Voksa. Can you tell me who was in command of the army forces.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Of the units --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, to expedite matters, my specific question is: Who was in command of your unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: My immediate subordinate [as interpreted], Colonel Mladen Cirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you tell me whether anyone from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps commanded you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, it was a single chain of command. I was subordinate to the brigade commander, he was subordinate to the corps commander. There was no dual command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, in paragraph 4 the English says: "The order was signed by Colonel Mladen Cirkovic, who was my first superior and who commanded me ..." Now, that must be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, that is precise because we marked Exhibit Number 6D731, which is signed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's just described Colonel Cirkovic as his subordinate, according to the transcript. Line -- 33, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If -- with your leave I will clarify right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, there's an error in the transcript. For the sake of precision, who was your superior? Who issued tasks to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: As it says here, this order was signed by Colonel Mladen Cirkovic, who was my immediate superior, and I was his immediate subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to these questions, who did you report to? Who did you brief?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I was constantly in touch with him on a direct line, round the clock. He had the same map he had given to me and reporting was done by means of that coded map and the phrase book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what was your duty in early 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: When I handed over the duty of the commander of the third group of the 15th Brigade, as of the 13th of January I think I was transferred to the command of the Pristina Corps and appointed chief of the training department of that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In that period, how was training conducted?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: There was a directive concerning training and there were orders. In view of the specific situation in Kosovo and Metohija, we received -- soldiers were sent to us who had already completed the first stage of training. After one month and 21 days they came to their units in the Pristina Corps, and then we continued training. That was the unit training stage, and it was training of squads and platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is your military specialty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: After completing the military academy, I became an artillery rocket unit officer for anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. In this officer [as interpreted] we have heard testimony from Prosecution witnesses, in particular Colonel Crosland, who said that the use of anti-aircraft guns to target land targets is not permitted, that it's even banned by the Geneva Convention. Can you tell me whether this is correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: In the course of my training on two occasions I had to pass exams on international laws of war. The only limitation on the use of anti-aircraft guns related to shooting at parachute targets and not all, but only parachutists abandoning damaged aircraft. They were exempt from the right of shooting with an anti-aircraft gun. That's how it was up to 1999. If something has been amended in the law since that time, I'm not informed of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, can anti-aircraft guns be used to fire at targets on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: In terms of how they're built, the possibility exists, but our training programme also comprises firing at targets on the ground. This firing is always a drill and is used to prepare our forces for firing at targets in the air. Whenever there is fire that is opened at targets on the ground, this is considered to be legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Defence Exhibit 5D1243. The e-court reference in the B/C/S is page 98. Can we please first see page 1, both in the English and the B/C/S. Page 1 in the B/C/S, too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, are you familiar with these rules?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I thank you for this unexpected promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, personally I would really like it if you could become a general --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't read too much into it because counsel call each other general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, are you familiar with these rules?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, rules for the 20/3 and 55A2B1 anti-aircraft gun, this one has no computer and has three barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we have page number 98 in B/C/S and in English, next one. We need paragraph 258 in English is on second page. [Interpretation] Again, the previous page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see both pages in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Here we go, Colonel. It's right in front of you. Can you please look at paragraph 258 of this document, which says that: "Moving ground targets and fixed targets when necessary can be fired at and water targets as well." Does that confirm what you said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this is clearly defined here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that in the English and in the B/C/S if we could please go to page 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you see 272 and 273 and so on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: If you call me general another time, that probably means I'll eventually become one. Item 272 -- Paragraph 272 unequivocally shows how targets on the ground are fired at. It states quite literally "infantry."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to avoid opening further documents, this is exactly the same thing that is stated in the rules and the use of anti-aircraft weapons, 5D1244, and rules governing the use of the 30/2 millimetres and 5335/7, 5D1245. Thank you very much. May I continue? Can we please have 424 on our screens, 5D424.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this document to come up, will you tell me -- there, you see the document, it's on our screens now. Item 2 says: "The necessity to harmonise and unite forces and PVO, anti-aircraft defence ... " Can you tell us what this means, uniting these in terms of anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I did this back in school, PVO systems, anti-aircraft systems, how they're run and how they're controlled. There's always the tendency that all the equipment that exists in a certain area is used together or united. There is a difference between troop anti-aircraft defence and territorial anti-aircraft defence. This was a request that we made to the effect that all these forces in Kosovo and Metohija, the rocket units, the territorial PVO, the fighter planes of the PVO, that these all be united and that a joint location be established where all of these would be together in one place to control the firing of their units. The objective of all this being to use to the best possible effect the features that these weapons possess and the systems that are in our possession and to exchange directly information on what is going on in the air-space. We normally referred to this as a joint command post because we were all independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Colonel, if you look at paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go to paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- you said that you took over from Lieutenant-Colonel Milentijevic, who was replaced and arrested because he was held to be personally responsible for the situation in the brigade. What I want to know is did you personally have any of the officers in the brigade replaced when you took up your post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, a number of officers were replaced. Sometimes the reason was that an officer was unable to perform his duty. I think there were five company commanders that I personally had replaced and also made proposals to the superior command about a particular battalion commander from the 1st Battalion, and General Lazarevic adopted my explanation and a major was dispatched from the corps command to replace this officer. So this was not a normal situation but this was something that happened every once in a while when a certain officer holding a certain establishment post failed to comply with his duties and obligations under the establishment or his functional obligations, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, did you take any measures with regard to any soldiers, ordinary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, whenever the conditions suggested that disciplinary infractions had been committed, minor infractions, if you like, some disciplinary infractions that the military disciplinary court would have been in charge of, I would take measures, I would bring them in, I would detain them, I would question them, and of course needless to say as the commander of a wartime Brigade, I had the right to keep soldiers in my own unit detained for up to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I simply need to ask you this: How many did you actually have detained at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: This is a step that nobody much liked at the time. It wasn't a very popular measure, but sometimes there would be as many as 15, 20, sometimes even 30 in detention on a given day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, given your level of training, given the positions you held in the corps, can you tell me this: Did the corps have any 545 or 556 or 12-millimetre calibre weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I was a head of the training section and I was familiar with all the calibres, all the weapons, and all the equipment that the corps had, some of these NATO calibres some were used by the former U.S.S.R.; and the answer is no under the establishment our officers had 7.65-millimetre pistols --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You don't have to go to all of this. I just asked you about those calibres and whether they in fact existed at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 5D1131, please. Just for the sake of clarity I don't think it comes across clearly on our screens these calibres. Was this just the corps or the army generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: There were none in the army, generally speaking. We have unified calibres in the army. The one that we use is 7.62-millimetres times 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Colonel, I think we actually have a translation for this document, at least that's what my associates are telling me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you care to share it with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just trying to check do we have in e-court system translation of this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There appears to be no translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to show just one paragraph of this document. It is so important for Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, no objection is being taken, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, will you tell me if you are familiar with this document that you can see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: If you look at item 2.1, I am here reporting to the corps commander on our activities as a brigade. The period that this dates back to is during an action known as Bajgora Dva. We searched the ground to the left of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity can you please read item 2.1 since there is no translation, no English translation, the first words are: "Situation," please read the document, first what the document is about in Item 2.1 because time is of the essence here.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I understand. This is a daily operations report to the brigade commander in relation to the 8th of May. Item 2.1, the situation and the activities of units --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down, slow down, slow down, I'll be speeding and you slow down.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The item reads: "During the day we carried out reconnaissance and we searched the Vlahinja Rusalja [phoen] road and the Cimil Dedinje [phoen] road. Pursuant to the commander's decision as set out in the task known as Bajgora 2. On that occasion in the Vlahinja village area, trig point 1012, and then the next word is detained, or taken in well that doesn't matter: 183 citizens, 14 men, 71 women, and 19 children from the woods" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm waiting for the interpreters to catch up.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: "These were sent to the school building in Vlahinja village where they were put up, given firewood to keep warm, and food. In the area" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's all we need. Thank you. That will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we interrupt there, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, we have to have a break at this stage; that will be for half an hour. While we have the break, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If I may, just briefly, I have two documents remaining that I still have no translation for that I would like to show the witness: One of these is 5D1132. Could that document please be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: It's a little difficult to look at because it's so small. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What's it about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: This is another daily operations report to the Pristina Corps commander, regular, daily report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we please go to paragraph 4 or item 4. Will you please read what it says.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Item 4 reads: "Morale. The situation in the units of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade is stable. It is affected in a favourable way by the capturing of the remaining members of the Siptar terrorist forces as well as by the commitment and discipline, as well as maximum compliance with international humanitarian law by our fighters who are responsible for the safety of over 200 persons of Albanian ethnicity who have been displaced and are now accommodated at the elementary school building in Vlahinja village."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, what sort of assistance did you provide to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I dispatched a medical team, there were two doctors, a male nurse and they examined those women and children who had applied for medical examination. We brought them firewood, and we brought them food. The locals themselves said that they had left behind some food in their homes. So at a later stage they simply thanked us and there was no further need for us to supply them with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any commendations by the 3rd Army commander of the Pristina Corps for what you did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The corps command received this report, and they in their turn reported to the army commander, and then the army commander sent a telegram to all the army units to point out what we did, and we were commended for our action in writing, which pleased us all a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to paragraph 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please read paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Sure. It reads: "Security situation because of individual cases of theft on private homes as well as desertion, the following were brought in: A soldier who left his unit without proper authorisation, two soldiers who committed theft from private homes."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you take vigorous measures in relation to all those who committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we most certainly did. There were disciplinary infractions, there were criminal offences, and in certain cases criminal reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last subject to discuss. I have two questions on that. Colonel, did the terrorists treat the wounded and killed in a monstrous fashion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict I viewed them as a legitimate opponent; however, on the 30th of May during the fighting near the Kolina feature, which is at a particular point along the Mitrovica-Klina road, there was this one particular wounded soldier whom they abducted from what we referred to as no-man's-land . The commander on the other side reported on this in the following way: We had been monitoring the radio communications, and that's how we found out about this. He said that he took one of my men and he was asking his superior officer whether he should bring this man to him. And then his superior officer said, No, just bring me his head. Two days later, as we continued fighting, further down the territory we found Ivan Milosevic's headless body. He was naked and we ascertained that he had a total of 29 stab wounds all over his body. Regardless of this, whenever we captured any of their fighters, we would dispatch them immediately to the Mitrovica hospital and there are documents to show this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Finally, can we please have 5D133. [In English] 5D1133, please. [Interpretation] Do you recognise this document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a daily operations report. The date is the 12th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we see count 5, I think that is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please read this for us, the first paragraph of item 5, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Sure. "All the security measures that had been planned and ordered are being properly implemented across the units in the sector covered by the 3rd Light Infantry Battalion in Vidusic [phoen] village a terrorist was wounded and was sent for treatment to the Kosovska Mitrovica hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you at all times provide medical assistance to those captured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, that was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Savic, my name is Dan Ivetic and I will be having some questions for you on behalf of Sreten Lukic. Now, first of all, I'd like to have you illustrate for us some matters. In paragraphs 15 through 18 of your statement you discuss in some detail the placement and activities of both your troops and the MUP forces taking part in the anti-terrorist action Bajgora Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time I would ask the usher's assistance because I will be handing a hard-copy of P1975 in the Serbian which is the order for this action and also an English copy, which I could ask to have 5.2 on the ELMO; so that while I'm showing you the map of e-court so if anyone wants, they can follow the English translation on the ELMO. Hopefully we can finish this and move on to the two other areas I have to question you on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
