utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I've given you the wrong period. Probably my question should have related to the whole period from then until -- that's from August until December.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was there a week. I was at our automatic firing range in Bijelo Polje near Pec. In view of the equipment I had available, the commander, who probably received an order from his commander, issued me with the task you have had an opportunity of seeing here in his order, and that was to support the MUP forces on the Decani-Voksa axis and the Crni Breg-Slup axis. In that action we had great losses and there was a very unpleasant episode concerning my command there and the support to the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You deal to quite a considerable extent with action along with units of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just as an example but I think it's a theme of your statement, if you look at paragraph 23 of your statement which deals with Prekaze, the last sentence says that: "During the execution of the task, good cooperation was established with members of the MUP." Can you give me examples of that good cooperation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, every well-implemented coordinated action requires good cooperation. My unit was threatened by stronger forces, stronger enemy forces, and so in spite of the task that the commander of the PJP detachment had been issued which had to do with the Mitrovica-Gornja Klina road, when I suffered losses at the Zmic feature I asked for help. He introduced first one company and then a second company to repel the enemy forces and the members of the PJP had losses on that occasion. I think a company commander or a platoon commander was killed. He was an officer. So we had three men killed in that action alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me an example in any action the other way -- where what happened was the other way around, that you gave support and assistance to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In the Bajgora 1 operation there was very strong resistance on the Majdan hill-Preten feature axis. And in the course of the night we provided support with mortar fire to the PJP forces which were under attack from the Siptar terrorist forces. Also, when advancing from the Bare village in the direction of Bajgora on the 1st of May or perhaps the 30th of April, there was a fierce counter attack against us on the forward companies of the 35th Detachment. And not only did we introduce all the reserves we had, but we also asked for assistance from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you provided mortar support, did they tell you the area in which they required that and the targets that you had to direct your attention to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the configuration of the terrain on which we were acting from the village of Bare towards Bajgora is a plateau where everything is visible. The support was direct, which means that the targets were visible, easy to see, and correction was possible. The range of the mortar I had at my disposal was 6 kilometres maximum, which means there was no danger of imperilling civilians, as there weren't any in the area. This was the last major counter attack in that area. One could clearly see all their units being brought in and taking up positions and their battle order and deployment. I don't know if I've managed to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was friendly fire on occasions a problem because you were each acting under separate commands?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No. Experience from 1998 taught me how to control and manage fire. So there was no danger of friendly fire. This was a success due to coordination and coordinated and concerted action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In general, though, was any particular step taken to avoid the risk of friendly fire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For every combat activity, whether in attack or defence, whatever kind of battle it is, a plan of fire support is entered into the map. So planned firing is entered into the map, and during the attack or defence when new targets are observed based on the map commands -- command is exerted and orders issued and the commander of the unit providing support is there with us. So we indicate to him the goal or the target to be neutralized or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there ever circumstances in which any item was warned to identify soldiers or others involved in activities as being part of the authority -- the official forces rather than any terrorist or insurgent body?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No. My men all wore the M-77 uniform and they were easy to recognise. The members of the PJP also wore the same uniform -- all of them were wearing the same uniform, so there was no danger of mistaking one unit for another and the enemy forces had those Chinese uniforms mostly. It was some sort of camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've been shown terrorists wearing or alleged terrorists wearing M-77 uniforms. You didn't experience that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Just one final matter then. The military -- the resubordination of a military territorial detachment to your brigade, who made the orders that gave effect to that resubordination?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the corps commander effected the resubordination of those military territorial detachments that had until then been part of military territorial departments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the military department commander also require to make an order to give effect to the resubordination?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: He had to issue an order because he also informed me which were the commanders of detachments, which forces and equipment they had, so he did issue his order on resubordination. But the military department was not resubordinated to me. It continued its regular activities. It only received an additional activity as commander of the Mitrovica garrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savic. Mr. -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one thing with respect to Your Honour's question, actually. At page 95, line 10, was warned to identify, I believe Your Honour said was warn, but I think you could clarify that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I did say was warn and I think the witness understood the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have a number of questions for you. My colleague Mr. Ivetic showed you a document of the command of the Pristina Corps showing the presence of your forces in mid-May in locations Gornje Zabare, Tamnik, and Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did your forces -- rather, were your forces in that area in mid-April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No. In mid-April they were not there. I have stated already that the entire brigade had not even been mobilised at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Ivetic has showed you the warning as you called it from the garrison commander, Colonel Nastic, from the month of May, warning all elements of defence. I would like to know who was in charge for law and order and the personal and security and the security of property?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior. In Mitrovica it was the secretariat for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were MUP forces perhaps resubordinated to Colonel Nastic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No. Both he and I had our own military police units that cooperated closely. Military police were responsible for military personnel and MUP was responsible for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up Exhibit P1975. You have seen this order already and we have discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You have it on paper. Very good. Tell me, which units received their tasks in item 5, or rather, which body, which agency?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: 211th Armoured Brigade, 15th Armoured Brigade, 58th Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was a single task issued to anyone outside the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Not in item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What does this document mean to you? Whose document is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Since it came from my superior command, I consider it to be a document of my command. That's how I understood it and how I implemented it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you understand by the term "supporting" in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, it can be fire support or logistical support. In this case it means to support with the resources available to the brigade, primarily fire support; and the rest of the support obtains when MUP units have executed their task and can cede their place to my units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you know when you read this what it is you've got to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we learned that at school. Support, air support, fire, artillery, moral and psychological support, logistical support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, which paragraph of this deals with your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 5.3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just a moment until I see the English. Now, that one actually tells you what you're supposed to do, but the ones we've been looking at don't. They don't say that there's a blockade, for example, to be set up. Now, if we go back to 5.2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5.2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, it does. My mistake. I hadn't seen that part properly. Thank you. And can we go to 5.1. Yeah. Thank you very much. Now it's clearer. I misunderstood it. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 71, 72 of the transcript, the Presiding Judge asked you a question -- I'm sorry, it was Ms. Kravetz from the Prosecution who asked that question in relation to coordination and you answered that someone higher should order with whom to effect coordination, meaning the commander of the Pristina Corps. Who is higher up and who can give orders to the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's easy, army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who can issue orders to the army commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the General Staff, or rather, if the war had already started, the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And would an outside body or a civilian person or any other agency issue orders to anyone in the chain of military command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was any sort of Joint Command able to give any orders to army units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: "Command" is a collective body, whereas our relations are based on single command and subordination. Command is where documents are drawn up in area a sense a commander commands not the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who is your commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: It was Colonel Cirkovic, Mladen Cirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your response to Mrs. Kravetz you allow the possibility that there was a Joint Command and now you gave me a different answer, so could you please explain? Was it possible for a Joint Command to exist and issue orders to General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: To allow the possibility is to accept something that is outside of my knowledge or control. It's not within my field of vision, so I allowed the possibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Listen to my question carefully. Was any sort of Joint Command outside the military chain of command able to issue orders to General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, after all these calls I finished I can say no. At that time I was at a lower level, battalion level. I didn't know what was going on higher up, but if we had been following the law then nobody could have issued orders to him apart from the supreme commander, who is also a military person, no Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, the members of the Supreme Defence Council, are they military people or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are civilians, but this is why there is a staff of the Supreme Command, manned by military personnel, which implements directives of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- yeah. We have I think a dispute in this case, though, about the power of the command staff and whether, in fact, the Chief of the General Staff as -- during wartime, and possibly also in peacetime, had any executive authority himself. So that's a matter that we will have to resolve in due course. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can intervene to hopefully correct the transcript. At -- one moment, please, lost it. At page 100, line 24, when referring to the Supreme Command in the B/C/S I believe the witness said he is also a civilian person not a military person, but we can have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it led me to ask a question I wouldn't otherwise have asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, you were asked: Was any sort of Joint Command outside the military chain of command able to issue orders to General Lazarevic? And you said that you didn't know what was going on higher up, but if we had been following the law then nobody could have issued orders to him apart from the supreme commander who is -- and you then told us whether he was a military person or a civilian person. Who did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We omitted one element. The commander of the army commanded over the corps commander, and he received orders from the chief of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're now losing the interpreter. You must speak a bit more slowly, please. All I want to know at this stage is what you said in your description of the supreme commander. Did you call him a military person or a civilian person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in all democratic societies at the head of the state is a civilian person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I will not let you go down any other road. Just answer my question. Did you say he was a military person or a civilian person? Now, if you can't remember, we'll have the interpreters tell us officially in a document which will be presented to the Court. All I want is your help, if you can give it, to save that work. You don't need to look at -- just tell me -- can you not remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I know what I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell me what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My commander of the corps was not commanded by a civilian. He did not receive orders from civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll order the CLSS to provide a formal translation; it's the only way to find out what you said. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could perhaps try to clarify this. You said that the corps commander was commanded by the commander of the 3rd Army, and who commanded the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: In peacetime the Chief of General Staff; in war, the Supreme Defence Council, that's the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope you don't think that's clarified it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, if I may ask some more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you feel you need to because you need to know the situation now, fine; but it will be resolved by a formal translation, although these do take some time, as you know. It's up to you. If you want to deal with it, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Colonel, what was the Supreme Command Staff in wartime conditions, what did it comprise?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff constitutes the Supreme Command Staff in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who commands it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Let's move on. Colonel, during Mr. Ivetic's examination you were shown a number of documents, P2809 and then the engagement plan and then your engagement plan and then these documents talk about the manner of engagement of the MUP forces after orders had been received from higher levels and the Supreme Command Staff from the command of the 3rd Army for the resubordination of the MUP. You told the President of this Trial Chamber that you had been expecting throughout the war that there would be resubordination. And what I'm asking you now is: Was there ever resubordination before the end of the war of the MUP forces to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, that never occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war you said that your command comprised officers from military territorial detachment, did you not? What about each of the resubordinated military territorial detachments, did each of them not have representatives in your command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They were commanders of the detachment, and from the command of the military department there had to be coordination with these detachments and there was an officer who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who was in command of the military detachments?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I myself directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Fine. That's what I wanted to know. General, can there be a collective form of a Joint Command in the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: No, that I can entirely rule out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And please tell me this, my last question: Who did you report to in the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: To the corps commander alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but in light of the witness's answers I'm obliged to pose some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the Supreme Command which hasn't been a part of his direct at all -- I need to clarify that because the evidence in this case has been quite different from what this witness is now saying and the defence of Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example of a question you want to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness should be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just tell me. No problem telling me the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, of course. Your Honour, the witness said the Supreme Defence Council is commanding the staff of the VJ. According to the constitution, we know what the constitutional provision. I don't want to give the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you think that we will be confused by what he said earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- well, I hope you will not be confused with what he said. I just -- because the transcript now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, on you go and ask what you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, just a single question. Are you familiar with the provision of Article 135 of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you before I've seen it, can you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have - I'm sorry I'm unprepared at this point - the constitution of FRY, what is the P number? It's 900 and something, 54, maybe, I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's P986 and 1D139. Let's have 1D139.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, while we're waiting for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we do not consider it necessary for you to explore this with the witness. We do not think harm will be done to your client's case by the answer that was given that concerns you, and that was the reference to the commander of the 3rd Army being commanded by the Supreme Defence Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. No, no, that the -- no -- how I understood the witness's testimony was that at the top of the chain of command was the Supreme Defence Council and that it -- that the Supreme Defence Council was commanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well -- that will not cause us any difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Then I don't have any questions of him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On reflection, Mr. Zecevic, I think that may be wrong because there is going to be other evidence in this case that could have an impact on this and indeed even expert evidence which may have an impact on it. And therefore it would be wrong for us to make assumptions based on what we've heard only so far. So yes, you should explore the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, are you familiar with the fact that singleness of command --, or rather, is singleness of command not one of the foundations of our military system?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that, subordination and singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain what the principle of single command and subordination means?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: What that means is that within the chain of command there is a single commander who issues orders, directives, that sort of thing, that's a single command, singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just check if my understanding is correct. A superior commander issues an order to a subordinate commander, so that's singleness of command, the relationship between two commanders, one superior, one subordinate, so that is the principle of singleness of command, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. I think that is the same as subordination, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: Subordination is the responsibility, or rather, the authority of whoever is issuing the order to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the screen in front of you, you see Article 135 of the constitution which reads: "In wartime and peacetime the Army of Yugoslavia shall be under the command of the president of the republic in accordance with a decision by the Supreme Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If my understanding is correct - and please correct me if I'm wrong - in order to implement the principle of singleness of command which exists in the army, it's the president which should exercise command, right, being the supreme commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: That's how it should be, but when you say for example in keeping with a decision, he exercises command in keeping with somebody's decision. I command, I carry out assignments based on a decision that is taken by my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I agree with you. In keeping with decisions, that means something very specific but I'm asking you about command, about exercising command. Who exercises command over the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR SAVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, does that raise any issues for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Savic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Zdravko Vintar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Zdravko Vintar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vintar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I just may put my glasses on. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to state your full name for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: My name is Zdravko Vintar, lieutenant-colonel in the Army of Serbia. I serve in the Nis garrison at the command of the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vintar. I apologise for interrupting you, but we have all of that in your statement and our time is limited and this is what I will be asking you. On the 25th of December, 2007, did you not make a written statement to the General Lazarevic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go through that statement, to re-read it and to familiarise yourself with its substance?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does your statement reflect everything that you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: Indeed it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were we to ask you the very same questions today, would you still provide the same answers that you gave as on the 25th of December, 2007, sir, the answers reflected in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: I would still provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this statement is Defence Exhibit 5D1394 and may it please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vintar, we have now dealt with this formality and we all have the statement before us. We know what it's about. There is no need for us to rehash what it says. I have no more than three or four additional questions or clarifications that I shall be seeking of you in relation to what you shared with us. If we look at paragraph 14 you state that in view of the fact that you served in Djakovica during the war, the NATO aviation spent a total of 42 days firing at the installations and units within Djakovica itself and in its immediately surroundings. You mention the Cabrat hill area and the old part of town, the Katovicka Street in the centre of town. We had a witness here Mr. Haxhibeqiri, who said that Stara Carsija and hadum, dzamija at the beginning of the NATO air-strikes had been set alight by the Serb forces. Please tell me whether any of that is true. And What about Stara Carsija and hadum, dzamija is this the old town and what about and Katalicka Street in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: That is the old part of town, yes; and it's just at the foot of Cabrat hill. On the very first day of the air-strikes, NATO fired at the barracks near the Erenik river. The distance from Stara Carsija is about 500 metres, and they fired at the slopes of Cabrat hill where our unit used to be positioned previously. I'm referring to 1998 when I say "previously." I remember that evening. I know that sometime after 2000 hours a fire broke out, and that part of town was soon ablaze. If I may just explain, this is a section of the town that was -- that mostly comprised wooden buildings, buildings made of wood. It's not necessary to explain is it. As soon as there is even a small explosion, these buildings will easily catch fire and also some powerlines that were just above caught fire too, some old powerlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me if there was a component of your own unit, the 52nd Rocket Artillery Brigade that was involved in putting that fire out and trying to repair some of the damage?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: What I know is that the fire protection squad was there and they had a fire engine, and they joined this operation in a bid to put out the fire. The town authorities also joined in. I'm not sure how successful they were, but I don't think they managed to achieve much since the fire was really raging and it was blazing away at great speed and it spread very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is Cabar hill the same as Cabrat hill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no Cabar, this is Cabrat hill, it's probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am also not understanding. Are you suggesting -- or at least I don't understand what you're suggesting the witness earlier in the case said, that's at line 10. Are you saying the witness said that something had been set alight by NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I see there is a mistake there. I said that there was a witness. I mentioned his name, who said that Stara Carsija had been burned or set fire to by the Serb forces, that was Fuat Haxhibeqiri and I asked the witness if he knew whether Katalicka Street and the old town, because that's was he said in paragraph 14, whether that was in reference to that part of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can see why the opposite impression had been created; however, you've clarified it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpretation was by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, if we look at paragraph 26 of your statement we see that you are commenting on a defence exhibit 5D1158. Can we just please have a brief look and I'll have an additional question about that exhibit. Sir, Lieutenant-Colonel, this is a regular combat report produced by your brigade, anti-aircraft defence. Can you please look at the last sentence of paragraph -- item 1, second paragraph, there is mention there of a NATO strike, they were firing at a column of refugees. And the last sentence claims that a team went out and an emergency team as well including a crew from GA Djakovica. What does this mean, GA Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: That is the garrison and medical station of Djakovica. It's a military medical station, and they were assisting those who suffered the consequences of the NATO strike when they fired at civilians. To the extent that I can now remember, on that day I was actually called by the brigade commander, and he told me about the air-strike and he told me that he had been tasked by the brigade commander to ensure that our brigade, too, the medical team from the medical station joined this campaign to provide assistance to those people. My task was to contact the municipal authorities to see if any further assistance was needed. I can't quite specifically remember now, but I don't think on that day I managed to get in touch with anyone because everybody was out in the field. The extent of this disaster was truly appalling and tragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, can you please clarify this: What about Cabrat hill above Djakovica before the war broke out and during the war, were there any tanks there, VJ tanks?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: On Cabrat hill there were the positions of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence and they had no tanks. The positions were taken up back in 1998. Just before the war broke out we moved the positions of our units because we expected that those would be targeted. We replaced these positions by mock positions with model equipment and model weapons, and we were successful in fooling the enemy fighter planes because they kept firing at those during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Lieutenant-Colonel, I just have a single question left. In paragraph 3 of your statement you say that the break-up of the SFRY found you serving as a battery commander, and you say pursuant to decision of the SFRY Presidency in July 1991 I declared myself willing to remain a member of the JNA. Can you please just simplify what kind of an order that was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: I'll tell you what this is about. After the conclusion of the clashes between the JNA and Slovenia's Territorial Defence, the Presidency of the SFRY adopted a decision for the JNA to withdraw from Slovenia's territory. That decision also made an option available to officers who were ethnic Slovenes to decide whether they wish to remain in the JNA or to go back to Slovenia. I submitted a written declaration to the fact that I wished to remain with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, back in 1998 and 1999, did you know of any plan, verbal or otherwise, or to expel ethnic Albanian civilians from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: I knew of no such plan to expel civilians from Kosovo and Metohija. I lived with my family in Djakovica, my wife, my son, my daughter in a residential building. Most of my neighbours were Albanian. I spoke to them both in 1998 and 1999, and our relationship was perfectly normal. I'm still in touch with those people, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about the VJ, to the extent that you're aware of it, your brigade, was it involved in a campaign to expel civilians on the ground I mean?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As an ethnic Slovene, you are still a member of the VJ, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: The Army of Serbia now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about 1998, had the army been involved in actions such as these against the civilian population, would you have remained its member?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO VINTAR
utterances.text: No, if the army had committed any crimes, I would have abandoned the army and I would have abandoned the country as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vintar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are all my questions. I really apologise for exceeding the mark, but I thought it more purseful to wrap up today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Vintar, we have to bring our proceedings for today to an end at this stage, and you have to return tomorrow to continue your evidence; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, it's vitally important that you have no communication at all with any other person about the evidence in this case, and by that I mean any of the evidence at any stage in the case. You can speak to whoever you like about whatever you like except the evidence. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.36 p.m.,
